evidence: Abstract and Secs.III-IV (pp.1-6): stability, local fidelity and interpretability of tree-ALIME vs ALIME on four tabular datasets (borderline: stability is one of three named outcomes)
read_from: arXiv:2204.03321 version of the CSICC 2022 paper (doi 10.1109/CSICC55295.2022.9780503)
problem: LIME-type explanations of neural networks need better stability, fidelity and interpretability.
method: tree-ALIME: autoencoder-based LIME (ALIME) with a decision tree instead of a linear local model; 10,000 Gaussian perturbations per instance; stability score on top positive/negative coefficients over repeated runs; human interpretability test.
data: Four tabular datasets (incl. a liver-patients dataset) and a sentiment text task (pp.2-6).
evaluation: Stability score over 20 runs with 20 different random seeds (pp.4–5), local fidelity, human prediction accuracy from explanations; comparison with ALIME.
findings: tree-ALIME gave significantly better stability and local fidelity than ALIME and improved interpretability (abstract; Sec.IV).
limitations: Authors: other tree models (e.g., random forest) left for future work (p.6). Ours: short conference paper; neural-network black boxes only.
qa_notes: Q2/Q3 brief; Q5 stability score loosely defined; Q6 small experiments; Q10 20 runs with 20 different random seeds explicitly reported (pp.4–5); reconsider the existing 0.5 score.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.III-IV (pp.1,4-9): stability, robustness and effectiveness of LIME, SHAP, Anchor, LORE and LEMNA on five Android-malware feature datasets
read_from: arXiv:2008.05895 version of the IEEE TIFS article (doi 10.1109/TIFS.2020.3021924)
problem: Analysts cannot tell whether explanation approaches for malware classifiers can be trusted.
method: Three quantitative metrics (stability across models/runs, robustness to adversarial-sample changes, effectiveness) applied to five explainers on classifiers for malware detection and family identification; top-k feature overlap for k = 1-20.
data: Five widely used Android-malware datasets built in different years (binary feature vectors, e.g., permissions and API calls) (p.1).
evaluation: Stability, robustness and effectiveness metrics; comparison across explainers and learning algorithms.
findings: Stability ranking LIME >= SHAP > Anchor > LORE > LEMNA; LIME and SHAP stability about 0.85; stability depends mainly on the explainer rather than the classifier (p.9).
limitations: Authors: threats to validity discussed (Sec.V). Ours: binary malware features; no prediction-preserving filter.
repro: Public malware datasets; code availability not checked in sections read.
qa_notes: Q8 not verified; Q10 repetitions not fully described in sections read.

evidence: Abstract, Secs.3-5 (pp.1-7): SHAP/LIME disagreement between prediction-equivalent models of different hypothesis classes on 24 tabular datasets, with theory
problem: Practice assumes that models with equivalent predictions give equivalent explanations.
method: Large empirical study of prediction-equivalent models from different hypothesis classes (tree-based, linear, neural); Spearman disagreement of SHAP (and LIME) vectors; Agreement Gap theorem linking disagreement to interaction density and axis-aligned tree splits (TreeSHAP interaction lemma); reliability score R(x).
data: 24 tabular datasets (MNIST only as a preliminary appendix extension) (pp.2,7).
evaluation: Lottery rate (instances with substantial disagreement, rho < 0.5), within- vs cross-class Spearman, Cohen's d; correlation with dimensionality.
findings: Prediction-equivalent models gave substantially different attributions; within-class rho = 1.000 vs cross-class 0.369 under split invariance; tree-linear agreement fell to 0.287 for d > 50 (r = -0.251, p < 0.001) (p.7).
limitations: Authors: within-neural instability not analysed (p.12). Ours: single-author preprint; disagreement across classes rather than perturbation stability.
repro: Reliability-score code shown in appendix; no repository link found.
qa_notes: Q8 code snippets only; Q10 multiple seeds controlled.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.2-3 (pp.1-8): SHAP importance across nearly optimal models with uncertainty intervals (ShapleyVIC) on tabular EHR data
problem: Explaining only the final model ignores the variability of SHAP importance across equally good models.
method: Generate nearly optimal models (loss-based Rashomon set) for an MLP by fine-tuning on diversified training subsets; SHAP global importance for each; uncertainty intervals and overall importance across models.
data: Electronic health records of 46,318 emergency-department patients admitted to Singapore General Hospital in 2017 (p.7).
evaluation: Distribution and uncertainty intervals of mean |SHAP| across nearly optimal models.
findings: Variable importance varied across nearly optimal models, and ShapleyVIC intervals gave a more robust picture than the single final model (abstract; Sec.3).
limitations: Authors: 'nearly optimal' defined by loss; extension to broader models planned (p.11). Ours: global importance only; one dataset.
qa_notes: Q4 compared with single model only; Q5 interval-based; Q6 one dataset; Q8 none found; Q9 ethics approval context; Q10 sampling of models described, seeds not.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.II-IV (pp.1-8): SHAP stability under Gaussian perturbation across DEM resolutions for LR, SVM, RF and XGBoost with repeated seeds (tabular slope-unit factors)
problem: Whether finer input data that improve predictive accuracy also improve explanation reliability.
method: Ten DEM-derived conditioning factors at 1-90 m resolutions aggregated to slope units; LR, SVM, RF, XGBoost under repeated random seeds; SHAP explanations scored for faithfulness, stability (attribution distance under Gaussian perturbation) and geomorphic consistency.
data: Event-based landslide inventory with slope units and DEMs resampled from a 1 m GF-7 DEM (pp.4-5).
evaluation: AUC-type performance; faithfulness, stability and geomorphic consistency across resolutions and models.
findings: Predictive performance and explanation reliability did not improve together; stability responded to resolution and model, and coarse DEMs could look stable by smoothing terrain while shifting feature-importance structure (abstract; p.7).
limitations: Authors: single event inventory; no spatial-block validation (p.18).
repro: Implementation details in appendix; code not checked.
qa_notes: Q8 not verified; Q10 repeated seeds.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.5-6 (pp.1-10): stability (Lipschitz estimate) of TreeSHAP, ensemble LIME and Anchors on MIMIC-IV mortality models (borderline: one of three criteria)
read_from: Publisher PDF (Int. J. Computer Sciences and Engineering 14(5), 2026, open access)
problem: Which post-hoc explanation method is most faithful, stable and comprehensible for ICU mortality prediction.
method: Gradient-boosting mortality models; TreeSHAP, ensemble LIME and Anchors compared on faithfulness (AOPC), stability (Lipschitz continuity estimate) and comprehensibility (explanation entropy/complexity).
evaluation: AOPC, Lipschitz estimate, explanation complexity, runtime.
findings: TreeSHAP had the best faithfulness (AOPC 0.276) and stability (Lipschitz estimate 0.312), with 4 ms per explanation; Anchors were most comprehensible (abstract).
limitations: Authors: single-institution MIMIC-IV data without external validation; structured first-24-hour EHR variables only; quantitative proxies and expert ratings without prospective clinical decision evaluation (pp.10–11). Ours: internally inconsistent Anchors AOPC and run-variance summaries (p.10); no identifiable code URL despite repository claims; repeated-model-run protocol not established.
repro: MIMIC-IV not redistributable; fixed seeds; no code link (p.6).
qa_notes: Q2 brief; Q6 single dataset; Q8 none; Q9 data-use agreement; Q10 fixed seeds only.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.2.2-4 (pp.1,4-13): stability, fidelity and regularity of NDT-LIME vs LIME surrogates on benchmark tabular datasets (borderline)
problem: Simple LIME surrogates are stable but cannot follow complex non-linear decision boundaries.
method: NDT-LIME: neural decision trees as LIME surrogates; stability = mean pairwise cosine similarity of explanations over R random perturbation runs; regularity across nearby real data points.
evaluation: Stability, fidelity and regularity scores vs linear and decision-tree surrogates.
findings: NDT-LIME improved fidelity on most benchmarks while trading some repeated-run stability for expressiveness; input-neighbor regularity was evaluated separately (Secs.3–4, Table 2).
limitations: Authors: higher expressiveness can reduce regularity (p.13).
qa_notes: Q3 dataset details in tables; Q7 brief; Q10 repeated perturbation runs.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.3-5 (pp.1-28): explanatory instability of local-linear and Shapley explanations tied to forecast uncertainty near segment/decision boundaries, tested in simulations
problem: LIME/SHAP-type explanations are unstable near decision boundaries, which is criticised in regulated credit settings.
method: Out-of-sample (OOS) Lipschitz and Hessian instability measures for local linear explanations and OOS Shapley values; conformal forecast-uncertainty; simulations with three data-generating functions and three model types (incl. gradient boosted trees, piecewise linear regression, sigmoid neural networks).
evaluation: Instability conditional on forecast-uncertainty region; one-sided Mann-Whitney tests (p.13).
findings: Instability was stochastically lower in low-uncertainty regions (p near zero in all cases); piecewise-linear models such as gradient boosted trees showed the same instability near segment boundaries as non-linear models (pp.2,20).
limitations: Ours: simulations only; single-author preprint; argues against seeking more stable explainers.
qa_notes: Q3 synthetic only; Q6 no real data; Q8 none; Q10 simulation design specified.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.3-5 (pp.1-15): probabilistic Shapley inference giving attribution distributions and credible intervals on synthetic and 8 real tabular datasets
problem: Point-estimate Shapley attributions ignore data noise, predictive uncertainty and their effect on attributions.
method: PSI: variational masking-based network that jointly learns a predictor and latent stochastic Shapley values (mean = Shapley value) with credible intervals.
data: Synthetic data and 8 real-world datasets (e.g., ICU, census) (p.15); MNIST encoded as patches (p.12).
evaluation: Predictive RMSE/PR-AUC vs baselines; recovery of true attributions and calibration of credible intervals in synthetic data.
findings: PSI matched strong baselines in prediction while learning attribution distributions whose intervals covered the true attributions in synthetic tests (pp.11,15).
limitations: Authors: constraint f_d = phi_d not enforced (Sec.5). Ours: self-explaining model rather than post-hoc SHAP.
qa_notes: Q5 uncertainty rather than stability; Q8 not verified; Q10 standard errors reported.

evidence: Abstract and Secs.3-5 (pp.1-7): SHAP-score intervals under uncertainty of the feature distribution, with a California Housing decision-tree case study
read_from: arXiv:2401.12731 version of the ECAI 2024 paper (doi 10.3233/FAIA240586)
problem: SHAP scores depend on an assumed feature distribution that is usually estimated, so rankings may be misleading.
method: Distributional uncertainty modelled as product distributions in a hyperrectangle; SHAP-score intervals and complexity results; case study with sampling at different proportions (5 repetitions).
data: California Housing (20,640 samples, 8 features, binarised) with a depth-limited decision tree (pp.5-6).
evaluation: SHAP intervals per feature; whether rankings change across the uncertainty region.
findings: Feature rankings stayed informative when the distribution uncertainty was small but SHAP intervals widened with fewer samples (p.6).
limitations: Authors: binary features and product distributions only; LIME/KernelSHAP left open (Conclusion).
repro: Code repository explicitly linked in p.5 footnote 9: https://git.exactas.uba.ar/scifuentes/fuzzyshapley ; repository accessibility and completeness not verified in this audit.
qa_notes: Q4 no explainer comparison; Q6 small case study; Q8 repository link present in p.5 footnote 9, access/completeness not verified; Q10 5 repetitions.
